source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77

coverage.included: A. Introduction and B.1 Nonjudicial Collection
coverage.note: Original ebook extraction has headings but not printed-page markers; page labels use syllabus range plus original § headings; separate distributed reading lists may later narrow coverage.

topics.title: A. Introduction — Creditor vs Debtor, Priorities, Human Capital and Timing
topics.description: Conceptual framework: why judgment does not equal collection, debtor versus third-party claims, consumer versus corporate relief, ex ante and ex post planning.

entries.title: Debt owed is not the same as money collected
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Proving liability and obtaining a judgment establish the debt, but collection law determines what assets can actually be reached.
entries.laymanExplanation: Winning a lawsuit doesn't put money in the bank if the debtor won't or can't pay.
entries.legalExplanation: Contracts and torts determine liability; debtors' and creditors' rights decide methods and limits of enforcement.
entries.examApplication: In any exam fact pattern distinguish validity of claim from collection tools and asset availability.
entries.examTrap: Judgment alone does not guarantee a priority lien in personal property.

entries.title: Two axes of debt-collection disputes
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Creditor versus debtor asks how payment may be compelled; creditor versus third parties asks who has superior claim to assets and is chiefly a priority question.
entries.laymanExplanation: First fight is getting your debtor to pay; second fight is beating other creditors or transferees to the property.
entries.legalExplanation: Analyze each separately: remedies, transfer avoidance, liens, timing and distribution.
entries.examApplication: For competing claims write parties, assets, time of rights, and applicable priority rule.
entries.examTrap: Do not decide a third-party priority case with only evidence debtor owes claimant money.

entries.title: Insolvency and allocation of scarcity
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Insolvency means assets insufficient to satisfy liabilities; not every creditor can be paid in full, forcing a distributive choice.
entries.laymanExplanation: There is not enough pie for all bills.
entries.legalExplanation: Outside bankruptcy first-in-time enforcement often governs; bankruptcy supplies collective distribution subject to secured and statutory priority.
entries.examApplication: State which creditors secured and which unsecured before assigning distribution.
entries.examTrap: Equal treatment in bankruptcy is NOT absolute.

entries.title: Individual debtor protections: exemptions, wages, discharge
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Human debtors retain limited exempt assets and wages needed for basic needs and future earnings; bankruptcy discharge can release many past debts.
entries.laymanExplanation: The law may let a person keep a place to live and enough earnings to rebuild, even if creditors lose money.
entries.legalExplanation: Human capital and dependents justify exemptions, federal/state garnishment restrictions, and individual fresh start.
entries.examApplication: Mention exemption §522, stay §362, discharge §727, where relevant, without prematurely assuming applicable chapter.
entries.examTrap: A corporation does not get the same human-welfare protections.

entries.title: Corporate debtor: going-concern value not a human fresh start
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: A company can dissolve after liquidation; Chapter 11 may be valuable if operating enterprise exceeds breakup value.
entries.laymanExplanation: The business matters because it could produce more alive than sold for parts.
entries.legalExplanation: Corporate relief is designed largely to preserve economically valuable operations; distinguishes individual debtor's human capital and survival needs.
entries.examApplication: Compare liquidation value with continued-operation value; identify employees and creditor recovery impacts.
entries.examTrap: Avoid treating corporate debt discharge as identical to an individual's fresh start.

entries.title: Speed and ex ante versus ex post planning
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Outside bankruptcy timing can fix lien priority; parties can obtain collateral in advance to avoid the unsecured race.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lender who negotiates security before trouble often beats a creditor trying to grab property later.
entries.legalExplanation: First-in-time/first-in-right, race of diligence and collateral agreements; bankruptcy tempers but adds its own timing rules.
entries.examApplication: Make a dated timeline, classify when rights attach and perfect, then ask effects of bankruptcy filing.
entries.examTrap: Earlier judgment does not always mean earlier lien.

topics.title: B.1(a)–(b) — Nonjudicial Collection, Tort Limits and FDCPA
topics.description: Leverage, tort liability, FDCPA scope and sections 804–814, Henson, Heintz, remedies and casebook Problems 1.1–1.2.

entries.title: Nonjudicial collection and permissible leverage
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Voluntary payment demands, bargaining and legitimate service leverage avoid litigation costs; abusive means may create tort and statutory liability.
entries.laymanExplanation: A creditor can ask for payment and warn it may sue, but cannot use every threatening tactic imaginable.
entries.legalExplanation: Unsecured creditors lack automatic right to seize collateral; secured creditors have property remedies; collection activities subject to tort and consumer-protection laws.
entries.examApplication: Classify caller, debt, conduct, and purpose before analyzing FDCPA.
entries.examTrap: Annoyance alone usually does not satisfy extreme/outrageous state tort tests.

entries.title: Tort remedies for extreme collections
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Extreme collection methods may involve invasion of privacy, IIED, defamation, assault, battery, interference with contract, malicious prosecution, conversion or fraud.
entries.laymanExplanation: False public shaming, physical intimidation or unlawful seizure can be torts even if bill is valid.
entries.legalExplanation: State tort liability depends on elements; legitimate creditor interest permits reasonable collection pressure, so mere embarrassment may not suffice.
entries.examApplication: Analyze actual tort elements and factual conduct separately from FDCPA.
entries.examTrap: The federal statute does not preempt all state tort causes.

entries.title: FDCPA coverage — debt collector and consumer debt
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: 15 U.S.C. §1692a(6) generally covers principal-purpose debt-collection businesses or those regularly collecting debts owed to another; §1692a(5) covers natural-person personal/family/household obligations.
entries.laymanExplanation: First ask whether collector and debt fit the statutory definitions.
entries.legalExplanation: A business/commercial debt and debt owed by corporation generally fall outside federal coverage; originators collecting own accounts often not within regularly-for-another prong.
entries.examApplication: Use four-stage issue tree: natural person, personal debt, actor definition (both prongs), wrongful conduct.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume being rude or collecting any 'debt' alone proves FDCPA applies.

entries.title: Henson v. Santander Consumer USA Inc., 137 S. Ct. 1718 (2017)
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: No, not on this argued prong: a debt purchaser collecting loans it now owns does not collect debts owed another. The Court expressly left principal-purpose statutory coverage unaddressed.
entries.laymanExplanation: An owner collecting an acquired debt for its own account falls outside regularly-for-another prong, but may still be covered if principal purpose is collecting debts.
entries.legalExplanation: Justice Gorsuch relied on statutory text; the phrase 'owed another' refers to who owns claim at collection, not whether purchaser originated debt or bought it after default. This ruling does not resolve independent principal-purpose prong.
entries.examApplication: Analyze purchased versus merely serviced obligations and the separate principal-purpose prong; compare lender collecting originally issued loan.
entries.examTrap: Incorrect to claim all debt buyers are categorically exempt from every FDCPA definition.
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt provided in Chapter 1
entries.facts: CitiFinancial originated car loans, borrowers defaulted, Santander acquired debts outright and collected the accounts for itself. Borrowers sued alleging FDCPA misconduct.
entries.issue: Does a company that buys previously defaulted loans and collects them for itself become a debt collector under the regularly-collects-debts-'owed another' phrase?
entries.holding: No, not on this argued prong: a debt purchaser collecting loans it now owns does not collect debts owed another. The Court expressly left principal-purpose statutory coverage unaddressed.
entries.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch relied on statutory text; the phrase 'owed another' refers to who owns claim at collection, not whether purchaser originated debt or bought it after default. This ruling does not resolve independent principal-purpose prong.
entries.rule: An owner collecting an acquired debt for its own account falls outside regularly-for-another prong, but may still be covered if principal purpose is collecting debts.

entries.title: Heintz: lawyers who regularly collect covered debts
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Heintz v Jenkins (1995) holds attorneys regularly pursuing consumer debt litigation for clients covered; Congress repealed specific attorney exemption in 1986.
entries.laymanExplanation: Collection lawyer cannot evade the statute just by filing a lawsuit.
entries.legalExplanation: A regularly employed collection attorney can be a debt collector and court filings and contacts may implicate FDCPA provisions.
entries.examApplication: Apply to Alice Attorney in Problem 1.1.
entries.examTrap: One isolated unrelated representation may not establish regular debt collection.

entries.title: FDCPA §805: inconvenient times, workplace and cease-contact demand
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: 15 U.S.C. §1692c restricts communications with consumer and third parties; §1692c(c) lets consumer request in writing that collector cease communications, with limited statutory exceptions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Stop calling someone's job after told calls are prohibited; written cease-contact request sharply limits calls.
entries.legalExplanation: Consider known inconvenient time/place, employer prohibitions, third-party disclosure, attorney representation, cease notice and exceptions for required notifications.
entries.examApplication: Apply to problems with work calls and midnight contact.
entries.examTrap: A valid formal demand and truthful threat to sue are not per se unlawful.

entries.title: FDCPA §§804, 806, 807 and 808 prohibited conduct
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: §1692b location inquiries constrained; §1692d forbids abusive harassment; §1692e forbids false/misleading methods; §1692f forbids unfair/unconscionable means.
entries.laymanExplanation: Calling six times in minutes, insulting a coworker or lying about legal threats can cross different sections.
entries.legalExplanation: Identify which provision fits each action; least-sophisticated-consumer perspective used for deceptive/harassing conduct as text describes.
entries.examApplication: Apply each of Problem 1.2(a)–(g) to relevant subsections and contextual facts.
entries.examTrap: Polite repeated calls may still be harassment; a truthful suit warning can be lawful.

entries.title: FDCPA §809 validation and debt dispute
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: 15 U.S.C. §1692g requires initial debt-related notices identifying creditor, amount and consumer's dispute/verification rights with statutory timing.
entries.laymanExplanation: Collector must tell debtor what debt it means and how to challenge it.
entries.legalExplanation: Validation duties, 30-day dispute window and collector's obligations need close statutory analysis; see Problem 1.2(f).
entries.examApplication: Distinguish timing of initial telephone call and subsequent written notice.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat 'within 30 days' as general ban on all contact.

entries.title: FDCPA §§810–812: payment allocation, venue and forms
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Act governs allocation among disputed/multiple debts, where collection suits may be filed, and fake forms suggesting uninvolved third parties.
entries.laymanExplanation: Collectors cannot game a consumer's payment, choose improper courthouse, or impersonate another participant through forms.
entries.legalExplanation: §§1692h–j impose distinct conduct requirements beyond generic harassment prohibition.
entries.examApplication: If fact pattern has multiple accounts/venue/impersonation, map to distinct statutory rule.
entries.examTrap: Avoid relying only on §§806–808.

entries.title: FDCPA private remedies and bona fide error
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: 15 U.S.C. §1692k provides actual damages + individual statutory damages up to $1,000 + fees/costs; class damages named plaintiff max $1,000 and other class members lesser of $500k or 1% net worth. §1692k(c) safe harbor for unintentional bona fide error despite preventive procedures; suit within one year.
entries.laymanExplanation: Debtor can sue for injury, up to $1,000 statutory penalty and attorney fees; inadvertent isolated clerical error may be excused.
entries.legalExplanation: Private litigation plus administrative FTC enforcement under §1692l; precise caps, burden and deadlines matter.
entries.examApplication: Separate compensatory/statutory/class damage buckets and test bona fide error elements.
entries.examTrap: A 'good faith' label alone is not sufficient if no reasonably adapted procedures.

topics.title: B.1(c) — Security Interests, Repossession, Sale and Deficiency
topics.description: UCC Article 9 self-help and judicial repo, no breach of peace, commercially reasonable disposition, waterfall, deficiency arithmetic and Problems 1.3–1.5.

entries.title: Secured vs unsecured creditor at default
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Secured creditor holds collateral enforceable through foreclosure, while unsecured creditor has no property right until judgment and appropriate lien.
entries.laymanExplanation: Bank with car lien can repo; ordinary unpaid medical creditor cannot simply take vehicle.
entries.legalExplanation: Personal property security interests under UCC Article 9; mortgage/deed of trust for land.
entries.examApplication: Identify collateral, perfection, default and competing senior liens.
entries.examTrap: Owning a debt doesn't itself establish collateral.

entries.title: UCC §9-609: self-help only without breach of peace
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Following default creditor may recover collateral through court or nonjudicially only if it proceeds without breach of peace; entry into home/restricted place and debtor objection are strong breach factors.
entries.laymanExplanation: Repo man may tow an unattended car in open driveway, but cannot force entry into locked home or push past objecting owner.
entries.legalExplanation: Consent voluntarily given at time often permits entry; advance boilerplate agreement disputed; false representation as police officer may invalidate consent.
entries.examApplication: For 1.3 analyze location, presence, resistance, consent, force, officer impersonation and timing.
entries.examTrap: Unwatched unlocked door does NOT mean implied consent to enter a dwelling.

entries.title: UCC §§9-610, 9-615: commercially reasonable sale and distribution
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Disposition after repossession must be commercially reasonable. Proceeds generally pay proper reasonable sale expenses first, foreclosing creditor next, subordinate secured interests next, then residual to debtor; senior security interests can survive sale.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell the seized item fairly; pay costs, senior foreclosing claim, juniors, then any extra to debtor.
entries.legalExplanation: Expenses may include authorized legal costs; Article 9 statutory ordering and lien seniority shape outcome.
entries.examApplication: Calculate exact debt, eligible sale costs, lien ordering and residual or deficiency; note surviving senior rights.
entries.examTrap: Gross sale price is not all applied to principal, and not every junior automatically gets paid.

entries.title: Deficiency and commercially unreasonable sale
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: If collateral sale proceeds insufficient, debtor ordinarily owes deficiency. In non-consumer Article 9, §9-626 rebuttable presumption caps by amount compliant sale would realize; consumer deficiency treatment left to state law.
entries.laymanExplanation: If $900 sale doesn't cover debt plus permitted costs, shortfall might survive; an unfair sale can reduce or eliminate recovery.
entries.legalExplanation: Creditor's UCC notice and commercial reasonableness duties affect deficiency; states differ for consumer sale.
entries.examApplication: Problems 1.4 and 1.5 require sale waterfall and separate missing-notice issue.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume identical consumer and non-consumer penalties.

entries.title: UCC §9-625 and wrongful repo liability
entries.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77
entries.summary: Breach of peace and noncompliance can expose secured party to statutory damages, tort damages, criminal consequences and consumer deficiency consequences.
entries.laymanExplanation: A bad repo may cost the collector more than it recovers.
entries.legalExplanation: Separate wrongful entry/false arrest/conversion of personal effects from failure to send sale notification.
entries.examApplication: When repo includes belongings or creditor claims police status, analyze multiple liabilities.
entries.examTrap: No one right to repo by force just because loan defaulted.

problems.title: Problem 1.1
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77 (B.1(a)–(b) — Nonjudicial Collection, Tort Limits and FDCPA)
problems.prompt: Five FDCPA coverage subparts: (a) creditor calls buyer of $2k computer debt, (b) hired collection agency, (c) agency purchases debt, (d) attorney writes and sues for client, (e) agency pursues corporate family-owned debtor. For each, identify both debt and collector; explain missing facts (e.g., consumer vs business use, principal-purpose practice). Do NOT answer.

problems.title: Problem 1.2
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77 (B.1(a)–(b) — Nonjudicial Collection, Tort Limits and FDCPA)
problems.prompt: Seven alleged violations: work calls after notice, abusive coworker voicemail, midnight home call, six polite calls in 24 minutes, formal five-day attorney threat, mailed validation notice five days after phone contact, discounted offer to settle time-barred account. Identify specific FDCPA subsection and any missing facts without answering.

problems.title: Problem 1.3
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77 (B.1(c) — Security Interests, Repossession, Sale and Deficiency)
problems.prompt: Five breach-of-peace variations: unlocked empty home/piano; impersonating sheriff for consent; advance entry clause; quiet tow from attached open carport at 3am; son actively objects as tow begins. Analyze each separately; leave outcome unsolved.

problems.title: Problem 1.4
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77 (B.1(c) — Security Interests, Repossession, Sale and Deficiency)
problems.prompt: Debtor owes $1,000, creditor sells repossessed computer for $900; $100 authorized attorneys' fees, $100 sale expenses, junior secured party owed $400. Calculate distribution, foreclosing creditor deficiency and effect on junior, keeping analysis unsolved.

problems.title: Problem 1.5
problems.source: Tabb & Brubaker, Bankruptcy Law: Principles, Policies, and Practice (5th ed. 2021), Ch. 1 (user-provided full chapter); Prof. Effross Fall 2026 syllabus pp. 1–77 (B.1(c) — Security Interests, Repossession, Sale and Deficiency)
problems.prompt: Same as Problem 1.4, but foreclosing creditor failed to give debtor required UCC §9-611 sale notice. Determine deficiency treatment and whether more facts about consumer status/commercial reasonableness needed; leave unsolved.
